questions.question: Which of the following is the correct sequence of events in flowering plant reproduction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pollination → Fertilisation → Embryo → Seedling**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pollination:** The process begins with **pollination**, where the pollen grains are transferred from the anther (male part) of a flower to the stigma (female part). This process can occur through various agents such as wind, water, insects, or animals. This step is vital for sexual reproduction in flowering plants.
 
• **Fertilisation:** After successful pollination, fertilisation occurs. The pollen grain germinates on the stigma, and the pollen tube grows down the style into the ovary. The male gamete fuses with the female gamete (egg) to form a zygote.
 
• **Embryo Formation:** The fertilised zygote develops into an embryo. This stage marks the beginning of the formation of a new plant. The embryo consists of the plumule, radicle, and cotyledons, which later give rise to the shoot, root, and seed storage tissue, respectively.
 
• **Seedling Development:** Once the embryo matures within the seed, it germinates under favourable conditions (water, temperature, oxygen) to form a seedling, which develops into a new plant. This marks the completion of the reproduction cycle in flowering plants.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pollination Types:**

 
 
• **Self-pollination:** Pollen from the anther is transferred to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
 
• **Cross-pollination:** Pollen is transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. Agents include insects, wind, and water.
 
 
 
• **Fertilisation Process:**
 
 
• Fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote.
 
• This process occurs within the ovule, which is housed in the ovary of the flower.
 
• Double fertilisation is unique to flowering plants, where one sperm fertilises the egg, forming the zygote, and the other sperm combines with polar nuclei to form the endosperm.
 
 
 
• **Seed and Embryo Development:**
 
 
• After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed, and the ovary becomes the fruit.
 
• The seed contains the embryo and stored food, surrounded by a protective seed coat.
 
 
 
• **Seed Germination:**
 
 
• Germination is the process where a seed develops into a seedling under favourable conditions.
 
• Essential factors include water, oxygen, and an appropriate temperature.
 
• During germination, the radicle (embryonic root) emerges first, followed by the plumule (embryonic shoot).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sequence of Events:** The correct sequence in the reproduction of flowering plants is **Pollination → Fertilisation → Embryo → Seedling**. Any deviation from this sequence will disrupt the reproductive cycle.
 
• **Role of Pollination:** Pollination is a pre-requisite for fertilisation. Without it, the male gametes cannot reach the female gametes.
 
• **Double Fertilisation:** Unique to angiosperms, where two fertilisation events occur: one forming the embryo and the other forming the endosperm, which nourishes the developing embryo.
 
• **Importance of Seed Germination:** Germination ensures the continuation of the species by giving rise to new plants under suitable conditions.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is TRUE about vasectomy?

options.text: It blocks the vas deferens to prevent sperm release.
It kills the sperm cells reaching the uterus.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It blocks the vas deferens to prevent sperm release.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vasectomy** is a surgical procedure performed on males as a method of permanent contraception. It involves cutting or blocking the **vas deferens**, which are the tubes that carry sperm from the testicles to the urethra.
 
• By blocking the vas deferens, **sperm cannot mix with the semen** that is ejaculated. This prevents the sperm from being released during ejaculation, making fertilization impossible.
 
• Unlike common misconceptions, vasectomy does not affect the production of the hormone **testosterone**. The testicles continue to produce testosterone, so male characteristics and sexual function remain unaffected.
 
• The procedure is typically performed under local anesthesia and is considered a **safe, effective, and minimally invasive procedure**. Recovery time is usually short, and complications are rare.
 
• It is important to note that vasectomy does not offer immediate contraception. **Residual sperm may still be present in the vas deferens** for a few weeks or months after the procedure. Therefore, alternative contraception methods are recommended until follow-up tests confirm the absence of sperm.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Testosterone Production:**

 
 
• The claim that vasectomy stops testosterone production is **false**. The testicles continue to produce testosterone after vasectomy, maintaining secondary sexual characteristics like facial hair, voice depth, and libido.
 
 
 
• **Seminal Vesicles:**
 
 
• Vasectomy does not involve the removal of seminal vesicles. These glands continue to function normally and produce seminal fluid, which constitutes the majority of the ejaculate.
 
 
 
• **Sperm and the Uterus:**
 
 
• The statement that vasectomy kills sperm cells reaching the uterus is incorrect. Vasectomy ensures that sperm do not even leave the male reproductive system, so they cannot reach the female uterus.
 
• The body naturally absorbs sperm that are produced after vasectomy since they are no longer transported via the vas deferens.
 
 
 
• **Effectiveness of Vasectomy:**
 
 
• Vasectomy is one of the most **effective methods of birth control**, with a success rate of over 99%. It is considered a permanent solution for those who do not wish to have more children.
 
• It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), so additional protection like condoms may still be necessary in certain situations.
 
 
 
• **Reversal of Vasectomy:**
 
 
• Although vasectomy is considered a permanent method of contraception, it can sometimes be reversed through a procedure called **vasovasostomy**. However, the success of reversal depends on factors such as the time elapsed since the vasectomy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Procedure and Recovery:**

 
 
• Vasectomy is a relatively simple outpatient procedure that typically takes about 15–30 minutes.
 
• Post-procedure care includes avoiding heavy physical activity for a few days and using an ice pack to reduce swelling or discomfort.
 
 
 
• **Prevalence:**
 
 
• Vasectomy is widely used as a method of contraception in several countries, including the **United States, Canada, and New Zealand**.
 
• According to the World Health Organization (WHO), vasectomy accounts for approximately **5–10%** of contraceptive use worldwide.
 
 
 
• **Counseling and Consent:**
 
 
• Before undergoing a vasectomy, individuals should receive proper counseling regarding its permanency and the need for follow-up testing to confirm its effectiveness.

questions.question: What type of bond is formed when a metal reacts with a non-metal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ionic bond**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An **ionic bond** is formed when a **metal reacts with a non-metal**. This bond occurs due to the transfer of electrons from the metal to the non-metal.
 
• Metals have a tendency to **lose electrons** and form positively charged ions (**cations**), while non-metals tend to **gain electrons** to form negatively charged ions (**anions**).
 
• The resulting electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions leads to the formation of an **ionic bond**.
 
• For example, in the case of **sodium chloride (NaCl)**, sodium (a metal) donates one electron to chlorine (a non-metal), resulting in the formation of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
 
• Ionic bonds are typically strong and result in the formation of crystalline structures, such as salt crystals, which have high melting and boiling points.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Covalent bond:**

 
 
• A **covalent bond** is formed when two non-metals share electrons to achieve stability. This type of bond does not involve the transfer of electrons.
 
• For example, in a water molecule (H₂O), oxygen and hydrogen share electrons to form covalent bonds.
 
• Covalent bonds generally result in the formation of molecules with lower melting and boiling points compared to ionic compounds.
 
 
 
• **Hydrogen bond:**
 
 
• A **hydrogen bond** is a weak bond that occurs between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (e.g., oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine) and another electronegative atom.
 
• Hydrogen bonding is responsible for many properties of water, such as its high boiling point and surface tension.
 
• This bond is not a type of ionic or covalent bond but a secondary interaction.
 
 
 
• **Metallic bond:**
 
 
• A **metallic bond** is formed between metal atoms. It involves a "sea of electrons" that are free to move around, providing metals with their characteristic properties, such as conductivity, malleability, and ductility.
 
• This bond is unique to metals and does not involve non-metals.
 
 
 
• **Examples of ionic compounds:**
 
 
• **Sodium chloride (NaCl)**: Common table salt formed by the ionic bond between sodium and chlorine.
 
• **Magnesium oxide (MgO)**: Formed by the ionic bond between magnesium and oxygen.
 
• **Calcium fluoride (CaF₂)**: Formed by the ionic bond between calcium and fluorine.

questions.question: Tooth enamel starts corroding when the pH in the mouth falls below _____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5.5**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Tooth enamel, the hardest substance in the human body, starts to corrode when the pH in the mouth drops below **5.5**. This is commonly referred to as the "critical pH" for enamel demineralization.
 
• At a pH below **5.5**, the acidic environment in the mouth begins to dissolve the calcium phosphate minerals present in the enamel, leading to dental erosion.
 
• Bacteria, especially Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus, produce acids as they metabolize sugars, which reduces the pH in the oral cavity. This is a major cause of enamel corrosion.
 
• The saliva in the mouth acts as a natural buffer to neutralize acids. However, when the acid production exceeds the buffering capacity of saliva, the pH falls below **5.5**, initiating enamel demineralization.
 
• Consuming acidic foods and beverages like citrus fruits, carbonated drinks, or sugary snacks can accelerate the drop in pH, increasing the risk of enamel erosion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of Tooth Enamel:**

 
 
• Tooth enamel is composed primarily of hydroxyapatite crystals, a form of calcium phosphate.
 
• It serves as a protective barrier for the underlying dentin and pulp, shielding the tooth from physical damage, temperature changes, and bacterial invasion.
 
• Enamel does not regenerate once damaged, making its protection crucial for maintaining oral health.
 
 
 
• **pH and Oral Health:**
 
 
• The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is alkaline.
 
• A healthy oral pH is typically around 6.8 to 7.4, which supports remineralization and inhibits bacterial growth.
 
• When the pH drops below 5.5, the conditions favor demineralization, leading to dental caries and enamel erosion.
 
 
 
• **Preventive Measures:**
 
 
• Reduce consumption of sugary and acidic foods/beverages to maintain a healthy oral pH.
 
• Practice good oral hygiene, such as brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and flossing to remove food particles and plaque.
 
• Use fluoride-based products, as fluoride strengthens enamel and enhances resistance to acid attacks.
 
• Chewing sugar-free gum can stimulate saliva production, which helps neutralize acids and restore pH balance.
 
 
 
• **Saliva’s Role:**
 
 
• Saliva contains minerals like calcium and phosphate, which aid in the remineralization of enamel.
 
• It has enzymes like amylase that help break down food particles and maintain oral health.
 
• Saliva also acts as a natural buffer to counteract acidic environments in the mouth.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Demineralization vs. Remineralization:**

 
 
• Demineralization occurs when acids dissolve the minerals in enamel, leading to erosion and cavities.
 
• Remineralization is the natural repair process where minerals like calcium and phosphate are redeposited into enamel.
 
• Fluoride plays a vital role in enhancing remineralization and preventing further decay.
 
 
 
• **Risk Factors for Enamel Erosion:**
 
 
• Frequent consumption of acidic foods and drinks, poor oral hygiene, and dry mouth conditions.
 
• Conditions like GERD (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease) can expose teeth to stomach acids, increasing the risk of erosion.
 
• Excessive brushing with abrasive toothpaste can also wear down enamel over time.
 
 
 
• **Fluoride’s Role:**
 
 
• Fluoride integrates into the enamel structure, forming fluoroapatite, which is more resistant to acids.
 
• Regular use of fluoride toothpaste and mouthwash significantly reduces the risk of cavities and enamel erosion.
 
 
 
• **pH Testing in Dentistry:**
 
 
• Modern dental practices use pH strips or advanced devices to monitor oral pH levels and assess enamel health.
 
• Patients with consistently low pH levels may be advised on dietary changes and oral care routines to prevent enamel damage.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding cell type and shape?

options.text: The white blood cell (WBC) has a round and fixed shape.
The nerve cell is long and branched in shape.
The red blood cell (RBC) is disc-shaped with a central depression.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The white blood cell (WBC) has a round and fixed shape.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The white blood cell (WBC) has a round and fixed shape:** This statement is **incorrect**. Unlike red blood cells (RBCs), WBCs do not have a fixed shape. They are highly flexible and capable of changing their shape to move through blood vessel walls and reach sites of infection or injury. This property, called **amoeboid movement**, allows them to perform their immune function effectively.
 
• **The muscle cell is spindle-shaped:** This statement is **correct**. Muscle cells, especially smooth muscle cells, are elongated and spindle-shaped to facilitate contraction and relaxation during various body functions, such as digestion and blood flow regulation.
 
• **The nerve cell is long and branched in shape:** This statement is **correct**. Nerve cells (neurons) are specialized for transmitting signals and are characterized by their long, branched structure, including dendrites (short branches) and axons (long branches). This shape ensures efficient communication across the nervous system.
 
• **The red blood cell (RBC) is disc-shaped with a central depression:** This statement is **correct**. RBCs have a biconcave disc shape with a central depression, which maximizes their surface area for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange and enables them to squeeze through narrow capillaries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **White Blood Cells (WBCs):**

 
 
• WBCs are part of the immune system and help the body fight infections.
 
• They exhibit **amoeboid movement** and can change shape to engulf pathogens through a process called **phagocytosis**.
 
• Types of WBCs include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils, each with specific immune functions.
 
 
 
• **Muscle Cells:**
 
 
• Muscle cells are specialized for contraction and movement.
 
• Smooth muscle cells, found in organs like the stomach and intestines, are spindle-shaped, while skeletal muscle cells are cylindrical and striated.
 
• Cardiac muscle cells are branched and connected by intercalated discs for synchronized contraction.
 
 
 
• **Nerve Cells (Neurons):**
 
 
• Neurons are the basic units of the nervous system, transmitting signals through electrical impulses.
 
• They have specialized structures, such as dendrites for receiving signals and axons for transmitting them.
 
• The synapse is the junction where neurons communicate with other neurons or target cells.
 
 
 
• **Red Blood Cells (RBCs):**
 
 
• RBCs contain **hemoglobin**, a protein responsible for oxygen transport.
 
• Their biconcave shape increases surface area and facilitates gas exchange.
 
• They lack a nucleus in mammals, allowing more space for hemoglobin but limiting their lifespan to about 120 days.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cell Shape and Function:**

 
 
• The shape of a cell is closely related to its function. For example, the biconcave shape of RBCs aids in oxygen transport, while the flexible shape of WBCs facilitates immune responses.
 
 
 
• **Other Examples of Cell Shapes:**
 
 
• **Platelets:** Small, irregularly shaped cell fragments involved in blood clotting.
 
• **Plant Cells:** Have a fixed rectangular shape due to a rigid cell wall, aiding in structural support.
 
• **Guard Cells:** Kidney-shaped cells in plants that regulate the opening and closing of stomata for gas exchange.
 
 
 
• **Diseases Related to Cell Shapes:**
 
 
• **Sickle Cell Anemia:** A genetic disorder where RBCs become crescent-shaped, reducing their oxygen-carrying capacity and causing blockages in blood vessels.
 
• **Leukemia:** A type of cancer involving abnormal proliferation of WBCs.

questions.question: Which wave characteristic determines the loudness of a sound?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Amplitude**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Loudness** of a sound is primarily determined by its **amplitude**, which refers to the height of the sound wave. The greater the amplitude, the louder the sound is perceived.
 
• **Amplitude** is a measure of the energy of the sound wave. When the amplitude increases, the energy carried by the wave also increases, resulting in higher sound intensity.
 
• Loudness is a subjective measure and depends on the sensitivity of the human ear. However, **higher amplitude** generally corresponds to higher loudness.
 
• For instance, in a graphical representation of sound waves, a wave with a larger peak-to-trough distance (amplitude) represents a louder sound compared to a wave with smaller amplitude.
 
• Amplitude is measured in **decibels (dB)**, which quantifies the intensity of the sound.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pitch:**

 
 
• The pitch of a sound is determined by its **frequency**, which is the number of vibrations per second. Higher frequency results in a higher-pitched sound, while lower frequency results in a lower-pitched sound.
 
• Pitch is measured in **hertz (Hz)**, and it does not directly affect the loudness of a sound.
 
 
 
• **Wavelength:**
 
 
• Wavelength refers to the distance between two consecutive crests or troughs in a sound wave. It is inversely proportional to the frequency of the wave.
 
• While it influences the type of sound, wavelength does not determine the loudness of a sound.
 
 
 
• **Frequency:**
 
 
• Frequency is the number of oscillations or cycles per second of a sound wave. It determines the pitch of the sound, not its loudness.
 
• A sound with a high frequency is perceived as a high-pitched sound, whereas a low-frequency sound is perceived as low-pitched.
 
 
 
• **Decibels (dB):**
 
 
• Decibels are the unit of measurement for sound intensity. A small increase in decibel level represents a significant increase in sound intensity.
 
• For example, normal conversation occurs at around 60 dB, while a rock concert can reach levels of 120 dB or more.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sound Waves:** Sound waves are mechanical waves that require a medium (like air, water, or solids) to travel. They are longitudinal waves, where the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave's propagation.
 
• **Human Hearing Range:** The average human ear can detect sounds in the frequency range of **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**. Sounds outside this range are inaudible to humans.
 
• **Resonance:** When an object vibrates at its natural frequency due to an external sound wave, it amplifies the sound. This phenomenon is called resonance and plays a role in enhancing sound loudness.
 
• **Threshold of Pain:** Loudness levels above 120 dB can cause pain or even damage to the human ear. Prolonged exposure to high decibel levels can lead to hearing loss.

questions.question: A student complains of difficulty in reading the blackboard clearly while sitting at the back of the class, but can read a book at 25 { cm} without difficulty. Which statement is correct for his condition?

options.text: He has myopia and needs a concave lens
He has hypermetropia and needs a convex lens
He has presbyopia and needs bifocals
He has cataract and needs surgery

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**He has myopia and needs a concave lens**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Myopia (Nearsightedness):** It is a common refractive error in which a person can see nearby objects clearly but has difficulty seeing distant objects. This is due to the light rays focusing in front of the retina instead of directly on it.
 
• **Symptoms of Myopia:** The student’s inability to read the blackboard clearly while sitting at the back of the class is a typical symptom of myopia. However, the ability to read a book clearly at a close distance (25 cm) confirms that near vision is unaffected.
 
• **Cause of Myopia:** It occurs due to either an elongated eyeball or an excessively curved cornea, leading to improper focusing of light rays on the retina.
 
• **Correction:** Myopia is corrected using a **concave lens** (diverging lens), which helps to diverge the light rays before they enter the eye, ensuring they focus directly on the retina instead of in front of it.
 
• **Age Factor:** Myopia is commonly detected in childhood or adolescence. It may stabilize or progress with age.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hypermetropia (Farsightedness):**

 
 
• In hypermetropia, a person can see distant objects clearly but has difficulty focusing on nearby objects. This condition is corrected using a **convex lens** (converging lens).
 
• It occurs when the eyeball is too short or the cornea has insufficient curvature, causing light rays to focus behind the retina.
 
• This condition is not applicable in the given scenario as the student can see nearby objects clearly.
 
 
 
• **Presbyopia:**
 
 
• This is an age-related condition typically occurring in individuals aged 40 and above. It leads to difficulty in focusing on nearby objects due to the loss of elasticity in the eye’s lens.
 
• It is corrected using bifocal lenses or progressive lenses, which aid both near and distant vision.
 
• The student in the question does not exhibit age-related symptoms, ruling out presbyopia.
 
 
 
• **Cataract:**
 
 
• A cataract is a condition where the eye’s lens becomes cloudy, leading to blurred vision. It is most common in older adults.
 
• Surgery is the only effective treatment for cataract, involving the replacement of the clouded lens with an artificial intraocular lens.
 
• The symptoms described in the question do not align with cataract-related vision issues.
 
 
 
• **Important Characteristics of a Concave Lens:**
 
 
• It is thinner at the center and thicker at the edges.
 
• It diverges light rays, making it suitable for correcting myopia by enabling light to focus correctly on the retina.
 
• Concave lenses are denoted with a negative power (e.g., -2.0 D).
 
 
 
• **Global Prevalence of Myopia:**
 
 
• Studies indicate that myopia is rapidly increasing worldwide, especially among children and adolescents. It is estimated that by 2050, half of the global population may be myopic.
 
• Factors contributing to this rise include increased screen time, reduced outdoor activities, and genetic predisposition.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Prevention of Myopia Progression:**

 
 
• Encourage children to spend more time outdoors as natural light may reduce the progression of myopia.
 
• Limit screen time and ensure proper lighting while reading or studying to reduce eye strain.
 
• Regular eye check-ups are crucial for early detection and management of refractive errors.
 
 
 
• **Advanced Treatments:**
 
 
• Orthokeratology (Ortho-K) involves wearing specialized contact lenses to reshape the cornea temporarily.
 
• Refractive surgery, such as LASIK, can permanently correct myopia for eligible candidates.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cell organelle?

It is a gel-like substance that fills the cell and acts as a medium in which cell organelles are suspended. • The cytoplasm is a part of the cell but does not perform specific functions like organelles such as the mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, or Golgi apparatus. • It serves as the site for numerous biochemical reactions and provides structural support to the cell. However, it is not considered an "organelle" since it does not have a membrane-bound structure. • **Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)**, **Mitochondria**, and **Golgi Apparatus** are true organelles, as they are membrane-bound and perform specialized functions within the cell. • The cytoplasm includes the cytosol (fluid portion), organelles, and other cellular components but is not categorized as a discrete organelle itself.

questions.question: Which metal will displace iron from iron sulfate solution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Zinc**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Zinc** can displace iron from iron sulfate solution because zinc is more reactive than iron according to the **reactivity series of metals**. This series ranks metals based on their ability to lose electrons and form positive ions.
 
• The **reactivity series** places zinc above iron, indicating that zinc has a greater tendency to form ions and can replace iron in a compound.
 
• When zinc is introduced into an iron sulfate solution, a **single displacement reaction** occurs, forming zinc sulfate and displacing iron. The chemical equation is:

 Zn + FeSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Fe.
 
• **Silver, Copper, and Chromium** cannot displace iron from iron sulfate solution because they are less reactive than iron. Their positions in the reactivity series are lower than that of iron, indicating their inability to replace iron in a compound.&

• **Isobutane**, as a branched-chain hydrocarbon, is used widely in industries such as refrigeration and as a precursor for making other chemicals.

questions.question: Which of the following statements best differentiates a compound from a solution?

options.text: A compound can be separated by physical methods, while a solution cannot.
A compound has a fixed composition and definite properties, unlike a solution.
Compounds are always liquid, but solutions can be in any state.
Compounds are mixtures of two or more elements, while solutions are mixtures of compounds only.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A compound has a fixed composition and definite properties, unlike a solution.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **compound** is a substance formed when two or more elements chemically combine in a fixed ratio. This fixed composition gives it unique and definite physical and chemical properties.
 
• A **solution** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances where the composition can vary. For example, you can have different concentrations of sugar dissolved in water.
 
• Unlike compounds, **solutions do not have fixed properties**. Their properties depend on the ratio of the solute to the solvent.
 
• The components of a compound are bonded chemically and cannot be separated by physical methods such as filtration or evaporation. **Solutions, on the other hand, can be separated using physical methods**, like distillation or evaporation.
 
• For example, **water (H₂O)** is a compound with a fixed composition of hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 ratio, whereas saltwater is a solution where the salt concentration can vary.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of a Compound:**

 
 
• Compounds have a **fixed composition**. For example, water always contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
 
• The properties of a compound are **different** from the properties of its constituent elements. For example, sodium (a reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) combine to form sodium chloride (common table salt).
 
• They are formed through **chemical bonds**, such as ionic or covalent bonds, and require chemical reactions to separate.
 
• Examples include **carbon dioxide (CO₂)**, **sodium chloride (NaCl)**, and **methane (CH₄)**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of a Solution:**
 
 
• Solutions are mixtures where the solute (e.g., salt) is completely dissolved in the solvent (e.g., water).
 
• They are **homogeneous**, meaning their composition is uniform throughout.
 
• Properties of solutions, such as boiling and freezing points, depend on the **concentration** of the solute.
 
• Examples include sugar water, saltwater, and alcohol mixed with water.
 
 
 
• **Differences Between Compounds and Solutions:**
 
 
• **Bonding:** Compounds involve chemical bonding, while solutions involve physical mixing without chemical bonding.
 
• **Separation:** Compounds require chemical methods for separation, while solutions can be separated by physical methods.
 
• **Properties:** Compounds have fixed properties, whereas solutions have variable properties depending on their composition.
 
• **Examples:** Compounds include water (H₂O) and ammonia (NH₃), while solutions include seawater and vinegar.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• Compounds are essential in **chemical reactions**, pharmaceuticals, and materials science.
 
• Solutions are widely used in **industrial processes**, medicine (e.g., saline solution), and food preparation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Misconceptions Clarified:**

 
 
• **Statement 1:** "A compound can be separated by physical methods, while a solution cannot." This is incorrect because compounds require chemical methods, not physical methods, for separation.
 
• **Statement 3:** "Compounds are always liquid, but solutions can be in any state." This is incorrect as compounds can exist in solid, liquid, or gaseous states.
 
• **Statement 4:** "Compounds are mixtures of two or more elements, while solutions are mixtures of compounds only." This is incorrect because compounds are not mixtures; they are chemically bonded substances.
 
 
 
• **Examples for Better Understanding:**
 
 
• **Compound:** Carbon dioxide (CO₂) used in soft drinks and fire extinguishers.
 
• **Solution:** Saltwater used in cooking and experiments.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct reason for why fruits fall from the tree when the branches of the tree are shaken vigorously?

options.text: The fruits fall down due to change in momentum.
The fruits fall down due to inertia.
The fruits fall down due to action reaction forces.
The fruits fall down due to frictional force.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The fruits fall down due to inertia.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Inertia:** When the tree branches are shaken vigorously, the branches experience motion due to external force, but the fruits resist this motion because of their **inertia**. Inertia is the property of an object to resist changes in its state of motion or rest.
 
• ** The shaking causes the branches to move rapidly back and forth, but the fruits attached to the branches remain in their initial position due to their inertia.
 
• Detachment of fruits:** The rapid motion of the branches creates a force that weakens the attachment of the fruits to the branches. When the force exceeds the strength of the attachment, the fruits detach and fall.
 
• **Newton's First Law:** This phenomenon is explained by Newton's First Law of Motion, which states that an object will remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force. The fruits initially remain at rest due to this principle.
 
• **Direction of motion:** Once detached, the fruits are influenced by gravity and fall vertically downward to the ground.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Inertia of Rest:** Inertia can be categorized into three types. In this case, the **inertia of rest** is relevant because the fruits initially remain at rest when the branches are shaken.
 
• **Newton's Laws:** The concept of inertia is a fundamental aspect of **Newton's First Law of Motion**, which is also known as the Law of Inertia. It explains why objects resist changes in their state of motion.
 
• **Example:** Similar examples of inertia include a passenger moving forward when a car suddenly stops or dust being removed from a carpet by vigorous shaking.
 
• **Gravity's Role:** Once the fruits detach from the branches, gravity acts upon them, causing them to accelerate downward at a rate of **9.8 m/s²**.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding inertia helps in various applications, such as designing safety features in vehicles (e.g., seat belts), understanding motion in sports, and analyzing forces in mechanical systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option Analysis:**

 
 
• **Option 1:** "The fruits fall down due to change in momentum" is incorrect because momentum involves mass and velocity, but here, the fruits are initially at rest.
 
• **Option 3:** "The fruits fall down due to action-reaction forces" is incorrect because while forces are involved, the primary reason is inertia, not action-reaction forces.
 
• **Option 4:** "The fruits fall down due to frictional force" is incorrect because friction opposes motion, and in this case, it does not play a significant role in the detachment of fruits.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Principle:** The phenomenon of fruits falling due to inertia is an excellent demonstration of Newtonian mechanics and the fundamental laws of motion.
 
• **Educational Context:** This concept is widely taught in physics to illustrate the principles of motion and forces.

questions.question: A student says, “Plants don’t have a nervous system, so they cannot respond to anything.” What would be the correct scientific response?

options.text: Plants respond using hormonal and electrical-chemical signals.
The student is right; plants are non-living.
Plants use nerves like animals do.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Plants respond using hormonal and electrical-chemical signals**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Plants do not have a nervous system like animals**. However, they can still respond to stimuli such as light, touch, gravity, and chemicals through alternative mechanisms.
 
• Plants primarily use **hormonal signals** (e.g., auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene, and abscisic acid) to coordinate their responses to environmental changes and internal cues.
 
• In addition to hormones, plants also utilize **electrical and chemical signaling** pathways for rapid communication across cells. For example, the closure of the Venus flytrap involves electrical signals known as action potentials.
 
• Specific examples of plant responses include phototropism (growth towards light), thigmotropism (response to touch), and gravitropism (response to gravity), all of which are regulated by these non-nervous mechanisms.
 
• Although plants lack a brain or nerves, their ability to adapt and respond to their environment demonstrates a highly evolved and efficient system of communication and response. *Hence, the student's statement that plants cannot respond to anything is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Plant Hormones:**

 
 
• **Auxins:** Control cell elongation, phototropism, and gravitropism. Example: bending of plants towards light.
 
• **Gibberellins:** Promote stem elongation, seed germination, and flowering.
 
• **Cytokinins:** Stimulate cell division and delay leaf aging.
 
• **Ethylene:** Regulates fruit ripening and response to mechanical stress.
 
• **Abscisic Acid (ABA):** Facilitates stomatal closure and induces dormancy during water stress.
 
 
 
• **Electrical Signaling in Plants:**
 
 
• Plants generate **action potentials** and electrical signals to transmit information across cells.
 
• For example, Mimosa pudica (touch-me-not plant) folds its leaves when touched, a reaction triggered by electrical signaling.
 
 
 
• **Phototropism:**
 
 
• Plants grow towards a light source due to the uneven distribution of auxins.
 
• Auxins accumulate on the shaded side of the plant, causing cells to elongate more on that side, bending the plant towards light.
 
 
 
• **Thigmotropism:**
 
 
• It is the response of plants to touch or physical contact. For example, climbing plants like pea plants curl around support structures.
 
• This response is mediated by differential cell growth and signaling mechanisms.
 
 
 
• **Gravitropism:**
 
 
• Roots grow downward (positive gravitropism), and shoots grow upward (negative gravitropism) due to the redistribution of auxins.
 
• Gravity-sensing cells in the root cap help direct this growth pattern.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Animal Nervous Systems:**

 
 
• Unlike animals, plants lack specialized organs like the brain or nerves for processing and transmitting information.
 
• However, plants rely on hormonal and signal transduction pathways to achieve similar adaptive responses to their environment.
 
 
 
• **Misconceptions:**
 
 
• The idea that plants are incapable of response arises from the absence of visible structures like nerves or muscles. However, scientific research has shown they possess sophisticated systems for perception and reaction.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Plant Responses:**
 
 
• Understanding plant responses aids in agriculture, allowing for improved crop management and stress resistance.
 
• For example, the knowledge of phototropism and gravitropism is applied in optimizing plant growth in controlled environments.

questions.question: During the transformation of energy from one form to another, such as gravitational potential energy converting into kinetic energy during free fall, ___________.

options.text: the total energy before and after the transformation remains the same
energy is gradually lost to the environment, violating the law
the total mechanical energy increases, adhering to the law
new energy is constantly created, balancing the loss of the original form

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the total energy before and after the transformation remains the same**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the transformation of energy from one form to another, such as **gravitational potential energy converting into kinetic energy** during free fall, the total energy in the system remains conserved.
 
• This principle is governed by the **Law of Conservation of Energy**, which states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.
 
• In the case of free fall, the **gravitational potential energy decreases** as the object falls, while the **kinetic energy increases** equivalently, keeping the total mechanical energy constant in the absence of external forces like air resistance.
 
• The total mechanical energy (sum of kinetic energy and potential energy) remains constant throughout the motion, provided there is no energy loss to external factors like friction or air drag. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• Options suggesting energy loss, increase in total energy, or creation of new energy violate the fundamental laws of physics and are incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Law of Conservation of Energy:**

 
 
• According to this law, the total energy in an isolated system remains constant over time.
 
• Energy can change forms, such as potential energy transforming into kinetic energy or heat energy, but the total quantity remains unchanged.
 
 
 
• **Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE):**
 
 
• GPE is the energy possessed by an object due to its position relative to a reference point, such as height above the ground.
 
• It is calculated using the formula: **GPE = mgh**, where **m** is mass, **g** is the gravitational acceleration (approximately 9.8 m/s²), and **h** is the height.
 
 
 
• **Kinetic Energy (KE):**
 
 
• KE is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion and is calculated using the formula: **KE = 1/2 mv²**, where **m** is mass and **v** is velocity.
 
• As an object falls, its velocity increases, causing an increase in kinetic energy.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Energy Conservation:**
 
 
• The principle of energy conservation is fundamental in various fields, including mechanics, thermodynamics, and electrical engineering.
 
• Examples include the functioning of pendulums, roller coasters, and hydroelectric power plants where potential energy converts to kinetic energy or electrical energy.
 
 
 
• **Role of Friction and Air Resistance:**
 
 
• In real-world scenarios, some energy is lost as heat or sound due to friction or air resistance, making the system non-conservative.
 
• However, in idealized cases (e.g., vacuum environments), the total mechanical energy remains completely conserved.

questions.question: The basic modification with a “prefix” or “suffix” in the nomenclature is the indicator of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nature of the Functional Group**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Prefixes** and **suffixes** are essential components in **chemical nomenclature**, particularly in organic chemistry. They indicate specific modifications based on the **functional group** present in the compound.
 
• The **functional group** is a specific group of atoms within a molecule that is responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of that molecule. Examples include alcohol (-OH), aldehyde (-CHO), carboxylic acid (-COOH), etc.
 
• In the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (**IUPAC**) system of nomenclature, a **prefix** is used to indicate substituents or side chains attached to the parent chain, while a **suffix** denotes the main functional group.
 
• The naming convention is hierarchical, where the **primary functional group** determines the suffix, and other substituents or groups are represented as prefixes.
 
• For example:

 - Methanol (CH₃OH): The suffix "-ol" indicates the presence of an alcohol functional group.

 - Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH): The suffix "-oic acid" indicates the presence of a carboxylic acid functional group.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nomenclature Rules in Organic Chemistry:**

 
 
• The **longest continuous carbon chain** is identified as the parent chain, and its name is used as the base name of the compound.
 
• The **functional group** with the highest priority (as per IUPAC hierarchy) dictates the suffix, while other substituents are named as prefixes.
 
• If multiple substituents are present, their positions are indicated with **numbers**, and the substituents are listed in alphabetical order.
 
• For example, 2-bromo-3-chloropentane has bromine and chlorine substituents at positions 2 and 3, respectively.
 
 
 
• **Common Functional Groups and Their Suffixes:**
 
 
• **Alcohol:** Suffix "-ol" (e.g., ethanol, methanol).
 
• **Aldehyde:** Suffix "-al" (e.g., formaldehyde, acetaldehyde).
 
• **Ketone:** Suffix "-one" (e.g., propanone, butanone).
 
• **Carboxylic Acid:** Suffix "-oic acid" (e.g., ethanoic acid).
 
• **Ester:** Suffix "-oate" (e.g., methyl ethanoate).
 
 
 
• **Importance of Functional Groups:**
 
 
• Functional groups determine the **chemical reactivity** and **physical properties** of compounds, such as solubility and boiling point.
 
• They are critical in **biochemistry** for understanding the structure and function of biomolecules like proteins, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids.
 
• For example, the hydroxyl group (-OH) in alcohols makes them polar and increases their solubility in water.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Functional Group Identification:**
 
 
• Widely used in **medicinal chemistry** to design drugs with specific biological activities.
 
• Helps in predicting the behavior of compounds in **chemical reactions**.
 
• Essential for **analytical techniques** like spectroscopy (e.g., IR, NMR) to identify substances based on their functional groups.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hierarchy of Functional Groups in IUPAC Nomenclature:**

 
 
• Functional groups are prioritized based on their reactivity and importance in the compound's structure.
 
• For example, carboxylic acids have higher priority over alcohols, ketones, and aldehydes.
 
• This hierarchy determines whether a group is named as a **suffix** or a **prefix** in the chemical name.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Prefixes:**
 
 
• Halogens like fluorine, chlorine, and bromine are named as prefixes (e.g., chloroform).
 
• Other groups like nitro (-NO₂) and alkyl groups (e.g., methyl, ethyl) are also used as prefixes.

questions.question: Which of the following types of human muscles show alternate light and dark bands when stained appropriately?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Skeletal muscles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Skeletal muscles** are also known as striated muscles because they exhibit alternate light and dark bands when stained appropriately under a microscope.
 
• These muscles are attached to bones and play a vital role in voluntary movements of the body.
 
• The striated appearance is due to the organized arrangement of actin and myosin filaments within the muscle fibers, which form repeating units called **sarcomeres**.
 
• Each sarcomere is bordered by Z-lines, and the alternating light (I-bands) and dark (A-bands) regions contribute to the characteristic striations.
 
• Unlike other muscle types, skeletal muscles are under voluntary control, meaning their movements are consciously regulated by the nervous system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Visceral muscles:**

 
 
• These are also known as smooth muscles and are found in the walls of internal organs such as the stomach, intestines, and blood vessels.
 
• They do not exhibit striations and are under involuntary control.
 
 
 
• **Muscles of the alimentary canal:**
 
 
• These are primarily smooth muscles that aid in the movement of food through peristalsis.
 
• They lack striations and function involuntarily.
 
 
 
• **Involuntary muscles:**
 
 
• This category includes both smooth muscles and cardiac muscles.
 
• Cardiac muscles are striated but function involuntarily, making them distinct from skeletal muscles.
 
 
 
• **Structure of skeletal muscles:**
 
 
• Skeletal muscles are composed of long, cylindrical fibers that are multinucleated.
 
• Each muscle fiber is surrounded by a plasma membrane known as the **sarcolemma**.
 
• These muscles are responsible for movements such as walking, running, and lifting objects.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Skeletal muscle examples:**

 
 
• Examples include biceps, triceps, deltoids, and quadriceps.
 
• These muscles are attached to the skeleton via tendons, allowing movement at the joints.
 
 
 
• **Cardiac muscles:**
 
 
• Cardiac muscles are striated like skeletal muscles but are involuntary in function.
 
• They are found exclusively in the heart and are responsible for pumping blood throughout the body.
 
 
 
• **Muscle contraction mechanism:**
 
 
• The sliding filament theory explains how muscles contract, with actin and myosin filaments sliding over each other to shorten the sarcomere.
 
• This process requires energy in the form of ATP and is regulated by calcium ions and the protein troponin.

questions.question: The size of the image formed by a convex mirror _________.

options.text: is always smaller than the object
is always equal to the object
can be larger or smaller depending on object position
is always larger than the object

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**is always smaller than the object**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **convex mirror**, also known as a diverging mirror, always forms a virtual, erect, and **smaller image** of the object irrespective of its position in front of the mirror.
 
• This is because convex mirrors have a **curved reflecting surface** that bulges outward, causing the reflected rays to diverge.
 
• The **image is formed behind the mirror**, and the size of the image is always reduced compared to the object's size.
 
• The nature of the image formed by a convex mirror is described using the mirror formula: **1/f = 1/v + 1/u**, where:
 
 
• **f** = focal length (positive for convex mirrors)
 
• **v** = image distance
 
• **u** = object distance
 
 
 
• Convex mirrors are widely used as **rear-view mirrors** in vehicles because they provide a wider field of view and always produce smaller, upright images of objects, enabling drivers to see more area.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Convex Mirrors:**

 
 
• Convex mirrors always produce a **virtual image** (an image that cannot be projected onto a screen).
 
• The image is always **erect (upright)** and smaller in size compared to the object.
 
• The focal length (**f**) of a convex mirror is positive because the focus lies on the same side as the reflected rays.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Convex Mirrors:**
 
 
• **Rear-view mirrors:** Used in vehicles to provide a wider field of view, helping drivers observe traffic conditions behind them.
 
• **Surveillance mirrors:** Installed in shops, warehouses, and parking lots to monitor activities in a large area.
 
• **Road safety:** Used at blind turns on roads to help drivers see oncoming traffic.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Concave Mirrors:**
 
 
• **Concave mirrors** can produce real and inverted images or virtual and erect images depending on the object's position relative to the focal point.
 
• In contrast, convex mirrors always produce virtual, erect, and smaller images regardless of the object's position.
 
 
 
• **Mirror Formula and Magnification:**
 
 
• The **mirror formula** is given as: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
 
• The **magnification (m)** is calculated as: m = h'/h = -v/u, where:
 
 
• **h'** = height of the image
 
• **h** = height of the object
 
• **v** = image distance
 
• **u** = object distance
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Convex Mirrors in Optics:**

 
 
• Convex mirrors are part of the **spherical mirror family**, which includes concave mirrors.
 
• Their **reflective surface bulges outward**, making them ideal for producing reduced, virtual images.
 
 
 
• **Usage in Daily Life:**
 
 
• Convex mirrors are commonly seen in **public spaces** such as stores and parking lots to enhance visibility.
 
• They are crucial for **road safety** at blind spots and intersections.

questions.question: Which type of cells are used by organisms like hydra for reproduction in the process budding?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Regenerative cells**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hydra**, a small freshwater organism, reproduces asexually through a process called **budding**. In this process, a new individual grows out of the body of the parent organism.
 
• The type of cells responsible for reproduction in Hydra during budding are **regenerative cells**, which have the ability to divide and differentiate into various cell types required for forming a new organism.
 
• **Regenerative cells** in Hydra are located in the body column and play a crucial role in regenerating missing tissues or developing new buds.
 
• These cells ensure that the new Hydra inherits a complete and functional body structure, including tentacles and the gastrovascular cavity.
 
• Unlike gametic cells, which are used in sexual reproduction, regenerative cells are involved in asexual reproduction, making budding a quick and efficient mode of reproduction for Hydra.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Budding Process in Hydra:**

 
 
• In budding, a small outgrowth or bud forms on the parent organism due to localized cell division at a particular spot.
 
• This bud grows gradually, developing structures like tentacles and a mouth, and eventually detaches from the parent to live as an independent organism.
 
 
 
• **Regenerative Cells in Other Organisms:**

• In humans, stem cells act as regenerative cells, aiding in tissue repair and development.

• **Gametic cells:** Involved in sexual reproduction, such as sperm and eggs, not used in asexual reproduction like budding.

• **Advantages of Asexual Reproduction in Hydra:**

• This ensures genetic diversity and survival in challenging environments.

questions.question: Why does ice float on the surface of water?

options.text: Because the density of ice is less than that of water
Because ice is at a lower temperature
Because it displaces water equal to its weight
Because the weight of ice is very small

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because the density of ice is less than that of water**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ice floats on water due to its lower density:** When water freezes, it expands and forms a crystalline structure that has more space between molecules. This increases the volume of ice, reducing its density compared to liquid water.
 
• **Density of water vs. ice:** The density of liquid water is approximately **1 g/cm³**, while the density of ice is about **0.92 g/cm³**. This lower density allows ice to float.
 
• **Hydrogen bonding:** Water molecules form hydrogen bonds in ice, creating a lattice structure. This structure is less compact than in liquid water, making ice less dense.
 
• **Buoyancy principle:** Ice displaces an amount of water equal to its weight, and since it is less dense, it floats on the surface of the water.
 
• **Thermal insulation effect:** Floating ice forms a layer on water bodies, preventing the water below from freezing completely. This is crucial for aquatic life survival during winters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Density:** Density is defined as mass per unit volume. For water, the maximum density occurs at **4°C**, and as it cools further, the density decreases as it transitions to ice.
 
• **Hydrogen Bonding in Water:** Water molecules are polar, and hydrogen bonding is responsible for the unique properties of water, including its lower density in the solid state (ice).
 
• **Role of Ice in the Environment:** Ice floating on water bodies acts as an insulator, protecting aquatic ecosystems by maintaining stable temperatures beneath the ice.
 
• **Applications:** This property of ice is vital for biological and environmental processes, such as the survival of aquatic organisms during freezing temperatures.
 
• **Other Substances:** Unlike water, most substances are denser in their solid state than in their liquid state. Water's behavior is an exception due to its molecular structure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 2 (Ice is at a lower temperature):** This is incorrect. While ice is colder than liquid water, its floating property is attributed to its lower density, not temperature.
 
• **Option 3 (Displaces water equal to its weight):** This is partially true but not the primary reason. The lower density of ice compared to water is the main factor enabling it to float.
 
• **Option 4 (Weight of ice is very small):** Incorrect. The weight of ice is not the determining factor; its density relative to water is what matters.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of Pressure?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pascal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **SI Unit of Pressure:** The SI unit of pressure is the **Pascal (Pa)**, named after the French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher Blaise Pascal.
 
• One Pascal is defined as the pressure exerted when a force of **1 Newton (N)** is applied uniformly over an area of **1 square meter (m²)**.
 
• Pressure is mathematically expressed as **P = F/A**, where P is pressure, F is force, and A is the area over which the force is applied.
 
• **Pascal Conversion:** 1 Pascal is equal to **1 N/m²**. In other units, 1 atmosphere (atm) is approximately **101,325 Pascals**, and 1 mmHg is approximately **133.322 Pascals**.
 
• Pascal is widely used in various fields, including physics, engineering, meteorology, and fluid mechanics, for measuring pressure in gases, liquids, and solids.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Units of Pressure:**

 
 
• **mmHg (millimeters of Mercury):** Commonly used in medical fields, especially in measuring blood pressure. 1 mmHg = 133.322 Pascals.
 
• **Atmosphere (atm):** Used in meteorology and scuba diving. 1 atm = 101,325 Pascals.
 
• **Torr:** Equivalent to 1 mmHg. It is often used in vacuum measurements. 1 Torr = 133.322 Pascals.
 
• **Bar:** Another unit of pressure used in meteorology and engineering. 1 bar = 100,000 Pascals.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Pressure Measurement:**
 
 
• In meteorology, pressure is used to measure atmospheric conditions, with instruments like barometers.
 
• In medical science, blood pressure is measured using units like mmHg.
 
• In engineering, pressure is crucial for designing hydraulic systems, aerodynamics, and structural integrity tests.
 
• In fluid mechanics, pressure is a key parameter in studying fluid behavior and dynamics.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:** Blaise Pascal's work in fluid mechanics and the study of pressure laid the groundwork for adopting the Pascal as the SI unit of pressure in the 20th century.
 
• **Important Conversion Factors:**
 
 
• 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101,325 Pascals.
 
• 1 bar = 100,000 Pascals.
 
• 1 psi (pound per square inch) = 6,894.76 Pascals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **SI Units:** The **International System of Units (SI)** is the globally accepted system for measuring physical quantities, ensuring uniformity and standardization worldwide.
 
• **Derived Units:** Pressure is a derived quantity in the SI system, expressed in terms of base SI units (kg·m⁻¹·s⁻²).
 
• **Relevance of Standard Units:** Standardized units like the Pascal ensure consistency in scientific research, industrial applications, and education.
 
• **Real-World Example:** The air pressure in car tires is often expressed in units like psi or bar, but it can be converted to Pascals for precise scientific calculations.

questions.question: What is the new Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio, set by the Reserve Bank of India for loans below ₹2.5 lakh in June 2025?

__
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, in its regulatory update for **June 2025**, has revised the **Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio** to **85%** for loans amounting to less than **₹2.5 lakh**.
 
• The primary objective of this adjustment is to facilitate easier **credit flow** to small-scale borrowers and individuals in the **unorganized sector** who require small-ticket funding for personal or business needs.
 
• By setting the **LTV at 85%**, the **RBI** has effectively reduced the margin requirement for borrowers to **15%**, allowing them to leverage a higher percentage of their collateral's value.
 
• This specific ratio applies to a variety of small-ticket credit products, including **gold loans** and micro-business loans, helping to drive **financial inclusion** across the country.
 
• The move is designed to mitigate the credit gap and provide a safety net for **micro-borrowers**, ensuring that they are not forced toward informal, high-interest money lenders.

__
 
• **Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio**:

 
 
• The **LTV ratio** is a critical financial metric used by lenders to assess the lending risk before approving a loan. It is calculated by dividing the loan amount by the **appraised value** of the asset being used as collateral.
 
• A higher **LTV ratio** (such as **85%**) means the borrower provides a smaller down payment, while a lower LTV provides a higher "equity cushion" for the bank.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**:
 
 
• Established on **April 1, 1935**, the **RBI** is India's central bank. It regulates the **monetary policy** and supervises the banking sector to maintain **financial stability**.
 
• The **RBI** uses regulatory tools like **LTV caps** to prevent over-leveraging in specific sectors like **housing**, **automobiles**, or **gold**, thereby protecting the health of the **banking system**.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Financial Inclusion**:
 
 
• By increasing the **LTV to 85%** for loans below **₹2.5 lakh**, the government and the **central bank** aim to empower the **Priority Sector**.
 
• This change particularly benefits **Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)** and low-income households, allowing them to access capital with minimal upfront equity.
 
 
 
• **Regulatory Guidelines and Risk Management**:
 
 
• While the **LTV** is increased to provide relief, the **RBI** mandates that banks and **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)** conduct rigorous **credit appraisals** and maintain **Capital Adequacy Ratios (CAR)**.
 
• The policy ensures that while credit is accessible, it does not lead to a rise in **Non-Performing Assets (NPAs)** within the financial ecosystem.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Threshold Limit**: The **85% LTV** specifically targets the "bottom of the pyramid" by capping the loan amount at **₹2.5 lakh**. Loans exceeding this amount are subject to different, often stricter, LTV guidelines.
 
• **Collateral Valuation**: Under **RBI guidelines**, lenders must follow a transparent process for valuing the collateral (like **gold jewellery** or **property**) to ensure the **85%** limit is applied accurately and ethically.
 
• **Implementation Date**: The new norms were highlighted as a key shift in the **RBI's June 2025** monetary policy review, reflecting the evolving economic landscape and the need for **liquidity support** in the micro-loan segment.

questions.question: Which of the following states/Union Territories has the largest number of wildlife sanctuaries as of 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andaman & Nicobar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Union Territory of **Andaman & Nicobar Islands** holds the distinction of having the largest number of wildlife sanctuaries in India, with a total of **96** sanctuaries as of **2023**.
 
• According to the **National Wildlife Database**, India has a total of **567 wildlife sanctuaries**, covering approximately **3.73%** of the country's total geographical area.
 
• The **Andaman & Nicobar Islands** account for a significant portion of these protected areas, despite having a relatively small landmass compared to large mainland states. ***Hence, the correct answer is Andaman & Nicobar.***
 
• These sanctuaries are vital for protecting the unique **marine life**, **tropical evergreen forests**, and **endemic species** like the **Andaman Wild Pig** and the **Narcondam Hornbill**.
 
• The **Wildlife Institute of India (WII)** and the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** are responsible for maintaining the records and overseeing the management of these protected areas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Wildlife Sanctuary (WLS):**

 
 
• A **Wildlife Sanctuary** is an area declared by the **State Government** or the **Central Government** under the **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** for the purpose of protecting, propagating, or developing wildlife or its environment.
 
• In a sanctuary, certain human activities such as **grazing**, **collection of minor forest produce**, and **private ownership rights** may be allowed as long as they do not interfere with the well-being of the animals.
 
 
 
• **State-wise Distribution:**
 
 
• **Maharashtra** follows Andaman & Nicobar with the second-highest number, hosting approximately **50** wildlife sanctuaries.
 
• **Uttar Pradesh** has **25** wildlife sanctuaries, including the famous **Hastinapur Wildlife Sanctuary**.
 
• **Kerala** manages **17** wildlife sanctuaries, such as the **Periyar Wildlife Sanctuary** and **Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary**.
 
• **West Bengal** contains **16** wildlife sanctuaries, including the **Sajnekhali Wildlife Sanctuary** situated within the **Sundarbans**.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Facts:**
 
 
• The total area covered by wildlife sanctuaries in India is about **122,564.53 square kilometers**.
 
• The **Rann of Kutch Wildlife Sanctuary** in **Gujarat** is one of the largest sanctuaries in terms of area, spanning over **7,500 square kilometers**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972:** This **Act** provides the legal framework for the protection of various species of wild animals and plants, the management of their habitats, and the regulation and control of trade in wild animals.
 
• **Difference between National Parks and Sanctuaries:** **National Parks** enjoy a higher degree of protection where no human activity or private rights are allowed, whereas **Wildlife Sanctuaries** permit limited human interference.
 
• **Conservation Status:** As of **December 2023**, India has **106 National Parks** and **567 Wildlife Sanctuaries**, contributing to the **Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats** scheme.
 
• **Endemic Species:** The high number of sanctuaries in **Andaman & Nicobar** is primarily due to the need to protect species that are not found anywhere else in the world (**endemic**), preserving the ecological balance of the **Bay of Bengal** region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Sorokhaibam Bindyarani Devi:**

• **Weightlifting Technicalities:**
